common_name: Elizabeth Traub Crinum (Fragrant Dark Rose-Pink Ellen Bosanquet Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant the large bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part sun; this 1930s Hamilton Traub hybrid of C. scabrum x Ellen Bosanquet is prized for its unusually tall, heavily flowered scapes.

directions: Elizabeth Traub was raised by Crinum breeder Hamilton Traub from a cross of Crinum scabrum and Ellen Bosanquet, and it carries the fragrance and dark color of its Ellen Bosanquet parent onto much taller scapes. Sturdy 4-foot stalks appear in early summer bearing 11 to 13 large, intensely fragrant, dark rose-pink flowers with a dramatic white throat, with scattered rebloom later in the season. Established clumps tolerate heat, humidity, and heavy soils with little care, making it a good fit for old-fashioned Southern perennial borders. Give it full sun to light shade and let the bulb stay undisturbed for years, since crowded clumps bloom best.

common_name: Walter Flory Crinum (Fragrant Bicolor Pink-Striped Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant in spring with the bulb neck at or just above the soil line in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; this Katherine Clint hybrid of Ellen Bosanquet x C. x powellii Alba is one of the earliest crinums to bloom each year.

directions: Named for Crinum taxonomist Dr. Walter Flory, this cultivar was hybridized by Katherine Clint from a cross of Ellen Bosanquet and Crinum x powellii Alba. It forms a relatively compact clump topped by 3.5-foot stalks carrying 13 to 15 sweetly fragrant, widely open pink flowers with darker pink stripes running down each petal. It inherits an early-flowering habit from Ellen Bosanquet, often opening its first scapes as early as April in the Deep South before a second flush in summer. Flowers can fade to a paler pink during the hottest part of summer, but the plant otherwise shrugs off heat and humidity.

common_name: Carroll Abbott Crinum (Improved Milk-and-Wine Lily with Burgundy Stripes)

planting.note: Plant in spring with the bulb neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part sun; this Texas milk-and-wine crinum was bred by Marcelle Sheppard from a cross of C. bulbispermum and C. scabrum.

directions: Bred by Texas hybridizer Marcelle Sheppard from Crinum bulbispermum crossed with C. scabrum, this cultivar is named for Carroll Abbott, founder of the Native Plant Society of Texas. It is an improved milk-and-wine type, producing 30-inch stalks topped with clusters of widely opened white flowers marked with a bold, deep burgundy band down the center of each petal, with several flowers per stalk facing upward. Thanks to its bulbispermum parentage it is one of the more cold-hardy named crinums, reported to survive winters into USDA zone 6 where the bulb is planted deeply and mulched. Like other milk-and-wine crinums, it tolerates heat, drought, and heavy clay once established.

common_name: Creole Lily (Crinum scabrum, Angolan Milk-and-Wine Species)

planting.note: Plant the bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this Angolan species is a parent of several Southern milk-and-wine crinum hybrids and needs more winter protection than its hardy hybrid offspring.

directions: Crinum scabrum is a milk-and-wine species from Angola, grown for flat rosettes of wide, glossy green foliage and midsummer stalks to about 30 inches topped with white, bell-shaped flowers marked by a bright red stripe down the center of each petal. It has long been used as a breeding parent for classic Southern milk-and-wine crinum hybrids and pass-along cultivars. Some taxonomists now treat it as a synonym of the wider-ranging Crinum ornatum, but nurseries continue to sell and label it as C. scabrum. It is less cold-hardy than its Gulf Coast hybrid descendants and appreciates a sheltered, frost-free spot with regular moisture through the growing season.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

common_name: Twelve Apostles Crinum (Old Pass-Along Bulbispermum x Asiaticum Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant the large bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained to moist soil in full sun; this very old pass-along hybrid of C. bulbispermum x C. asiaticum reliably repeat-blooms through the growing season.

directions: Twelve Apostles is an old Southern pass-along selection of Crinum x eboracii, a natural hybrid between the cold-hardy Crinum bulbispermum and the tropical Crinum asiaticum. It combines the bluish-gray foliage of its bulbispermum parent with the stiff, upright habit of asiaticum, sending up sturdy 4.5-foot spikes topped with large umbels of upward-facing, musky-fragrant white flowers washed with pinkish purple on the reverse. Once established it is a reliable repeat bloomer, typically flowering in spring, again in summer, and often once more in fall before frost. Like other bulbispermum hybrids it tolerates heat, drought, and heavy soils with minimal care.

common_name: Cheers Crinum (Burgundy-Backed White Variabile x Bulbispermum Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant the bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; this Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction blooms later in the season than most Southern pass-along crinums.

directions: Cheers is a 2019 Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights introduction selected from a cross of Crinum variabile and Crinum bulbispermum made by Indiana hybridizer Jim Shields. Starting in mid-August, sturdy 30-inch stalks carry 16 to 18 tubular flowers that open white on the inside while the reverse is flushed burgundy with dark burgundy keels, giving the flower clusters a two-toned look. It extends the crinum bloom season into late summer and fall, well after most spring- and early-summer-flowering pass-along cultivars have finished. Grow it the same as other hardy Southern crinum hybrids, in full sun with fertile, evenly moist soil.

common_name: Darling Lily (Crinum flaccidum, Australian Murray Lily)

planting.note: Plant the bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; this inland Australian species is killed by frost and needs a mild, frost-free site or winter protection.

directions: Also called the Darling lily or Murray lily, Crinum flaccidum grows wild along floodway rivers of inland eastern Australia, including the Darling, Murray, and Macquarie systems, where it tolerates both periodic flooding and long dry spells between floods. An egg-shaped bulb sends up flat, soft strap leaves and a cluster of 4 to 16 strongly scented, tubular white to creamy flowers atop a single stalk, usually triggered by rain after drought. It has little cold tolerance and is killed outright by hard frost, so in the garden it needs a mild, frost-free spot or should be lifted and stored over winter where freezes occur. It is best suited to gardeners in the warmest parts of the Gulf Coast and similar frost-free climates.

common_name: River Lily (Crinum pedunculatum, Australian Mangrove Lily)
subcategory: Australian coastal and mangrove-edge crinum species

planting.note: Plant the large bulb in spring in moist to poorly drained soil in full sun to part shade; this Australian coastal species grows naturally along tidal rivers and mangrove margins and only tolerates light frost.

directions: Known as the river lily, swamp lily, or mangrove lily, Crinum pedunculatum grows along tidal rivers, estuaries, and mangrove edges of coastal Queensland, New South Wales, and the Northern Territory. It is a large, strapping perennial, eventually reaching several feet tall and wide, with long, thick, blunt-tipped leaves and summer clusters of 10 to 25 fragrant white flowers. It tolerates poor drainage and heavy clay and grows well at the edge of ponds or in low, boggy spots, but only shrugs off light frost, so it is best reserved for the mildest Gulf Coast gardens or grown in containers that can be sheltered in winter.

common_name: Water Onion (Crinum thaianum, Thai Aquatic Crinum)

planting.note: Plant the onion-like bulb with about one-third above the substrate in a shallow pond, bog, or aquarium margin in full sun to part sun; this Thai endemic is grown as much for its long ribbon-like leaves as for its flowers.

directions: Crinum thaianum, the water onion, is native to fast-flowing coastal streams of Ranong and Phang Nga Provinces in southern Thailand, where habitat loss has made it increasingly rare in the wild. An onion-like bulb sends up very long, narrow, ribbon-like leaves and a tall stalk of white, lily-like flowers held above the water's surface. It is most often grown as a submerged or marginal aquatic plant in ponds and aquariums rather than a conventional border perennial, thriving in a nutrient-rich substrate with plenty of root room. It has no meaningful frost tolerance and must be kept in warm water or brought in for winter anywhere outside the mildest, frost-free zones.

planting.note: Plant the bulb in spring with its neck at or just above the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; this tropical Southeast Asian species has long been grown in Vietnam both as an ornamental and as a traditional medicinal herb.

directions: Crinum latifolium is a stout, rosette-forming species from Vietnam and neighboring parts of tropical Asia, with long, straplike leaves and umbels of sweetly fragrant, night-blooming white flowers held on stalks well above the foliage. In Vietnamese traditional medicine it is known as the Royal Female Herb and was historically reserved for the royal court, and its leaves remain widely studied and used today. As a garden plant it wants the same conditions as other tropical crinums: rich, well-drained soil, regular moisture, and full sun to light shade, with no tolerance for freezing temperatures. It is best grown in the warmest parts of the Gulf Coast or in a container that can be moved under cover for winter.
